bt67yj-a1e360.summary: Distinctio 37 of Estius's commentary on Book 1 covers the presence of God in creatures, in place, and in time across six capitula. It establishes from Scripture and the Fathers that God is everywhere, and sets out the threefold scholastic mode of presence (by power, by presence, by essence), using Cajetan's distinction between immediacy of virtue and immediacy of suppositum to separate power from essence (c.1). It adds a special graced indwelling in the just, which admits degrees and culminates uniquely in Christ through the hypostatic union (c.2). It distinguishes circumscriptive, definitive, and eminent being-in-place, proper respectively to bodies, angels, and God, and applies a parallel scheme to time, with God as immutable cause and measure (c.3). It argues that omnipresence in the proper sense belongs to God alone and cannot be communicated, which rules out the ubiquitarian doctrine of Christ's body (c.4). It denies that God was literally 'somewhere' before creation or is actually present in imaginary spaces beyond the world: God dwells in himself, and following Scotus and Bonaventure is at most potentially present there (c.5). It closes by explaining why God is not defiled by the things he is in, namely divine impassibility and sin understood as privation, which also exposes the root of the Manichaean denial of Christ's real flesh (c.6).
claims: God is truly present in all things, in three formally distinct general modes: by power, by presence, and by essence.
Beyond these general modes, God dwells specially by grace in the just, in degrees that culminate uniquely in Christ through the hypostatic union.
Bodies are in place circumscriptively, angels definitively, and God eminently, as the giver of being to place; a parallel scheme holds for time, where God is the immutable cause and measure.
Omnipresence in the proper sense (primary, whole, per se) is proper to God and cannot be communicated to any creature, including Christ's body, so ubiquitarianism is heretical.
God was nowhere before creation and is not actually present in imaginary spaces beyond the world; he dwells in himself and is at most potentially present there.
God's presence in all things does not defile him, because he is impassible and because sin, the only true uncleanness, is a privation that God does not cause.

bt67yj-a1e815.summary: Distinctio 44, the last distinction of Estius's commentary on Book 2, takes up two questions about power. Capitulum 1 asks whether the power to sin is from God. It distinguishes three senses: the natural faculty of the will, and the unimpeded power actually to carry out an act, are both from God, the latter through divine ordination and permission; defectibility, the creature's capacity to fall short of the right, is an impotence rather than a power and comes from the creature's origin ex nihilo, not from God. It also rejects a letter to Demetrias attributed to Augustine or Jerome as the work of Pelagius. Capitulum 2 asks whether it is ever lawful to resist authority. Authority taken abstractly is divinely ordained and can never be resisted. Taken concretely, in the people who hold it, obedience is owed absolutely within the bounds of their office. Commands beyond those bounds that are good or indifferent need not strictly be obeyed, though compliance is usually advisable to avoid scandal, and commands to do evil must always be refused. The collective body of a realm may sometimes resist or depose a tyrant, but no private person may forcibly resist, and no one may kill, even a tyrannical ruler.
claims: The power to sin must be taken in three senses: the natural faculty and the unimpeded power to act are from God, but defectibility is not.
Defectibility is an impotence rather than a potency, and it arises from the creature's being made from nothing.
Authority considered abstractly is divinely ordained and can never rightly be resisted.

Obedience is owed within a superior's proper authority; commands to do evil must never be obeyed, and commands beyond that authority that are good or indifferent bind only by reason of avoiding scandal.
A kingdom's collective body may sometimes resist or depose a tyrant, but private individuals may not forcibly resist and no one may kill even a tyrannical ruler.
concepts: collective vs. private resistance to tyranny

bt67yj-a1e61.summary: Partial summary: of the 48 distinctions of Estius's commentary on Book 1 of the Sentences, this entry rests only on Distinctio 37, the only one with interpretations so far, and must not be read as a summary of the whole book. Within that coverage, Book 1 treats the presence of God. God is in all things by power, presence, and essence, and dwells specially by grace in the just and supremely in Christ. God is in place and time eminently, as their cause and measure, unlike bodies (circumscriptively) and angels (definitively). Omnipresence cannot be communicated to any creature, which excludes ubiquitarianism. God is not actually present in imaginary spaces beyond the world but dwells in himself. His presence in all things leaves him undefiled, since he is impassible and sin is a privation.
claims: (From d.37) God is present in all things by power, presence, and essence, and specially by grace in the just, supremely in Christ.
(From d.37) God is in place and time eminently, as their cause and measure, and omnipresence in the proper sense cannot be communicated to any creature.
(From d.37) God is not actually present in imaginary spaces beyond the world, and his presence in creatures does not defile him.

bt67yj-a1e459.summary: Partial summary: of the 44 distinctions of Estius's commentary on Book 2 of the Sentences, this entry rests only on Distinctio 44, the last distinction, which is the only one with interpretations so far, and must not be read as a summary of the whole book. Within that coverage, Book 2 ends with two questions about power. The power to sin is from God as natural faculty and as unimpeded ability to act, but not as defectibility, which comes from the creature's being made from nothing. Authority is divinely ordained and owed obedience within its bounds, but never in commands to do evil. A realm acting collectively may sometimes resist or depose a tyrant, but private persons may not forcibly resist him and no one may kill him.
claims: (From d.44) The power to sin is from God as faculty and as unimpeded ability to act, but defectibility comes from the creature's origin ex nihilo.
(From d.44) Authority is divinely ordained and owed obedience within its bounds, but commands to do evil must be refused.
(From d.44) Collective resistance to or deposition of a tyrant may sometimes be just, but private forcible resistance and tyrannicide are never lawful.
concepts: collective vs. private resistance to tyranny

bt67yj.summary: Partial summary: this entry for Guillelmus Estius's Commentarius in Libros Sententiarum rests only on Liber 1, Distinctio 37 and Liber 2, Distinctio 44, the only distinctions with interpretations so far. It must not be read as a summary of the whole work. On that narrow basis, the commentary is a scholastic exposition of Lombard's Sentences, chapter by chapter. Estius weighs Scripture, the Fathers (especially Augustine), and scholastic authorities (Aquinas, Cajetan, Scotus, Bonaventure). He sorts out questions by drawing distinctions, and he sets his positions against heretical positions such as ubiquitarianism, Manichaeism, and Pelagianism. In Book 1 (d.37) he treats the modes of God's presence in creatures, place, and time, and holds that omnipresence belongs to God alone. In Book 2 (d.44) he treats whether the power to sin is from God and the limits of obedience to authority, including resistance to tyrants.
claims: (From l1d37) Omnipresence belongs properly to God alone, who is in all things by power, presence, and essence, and in place and time eminently.
(From l2d44) Defectibility, the root of the power to sin, comes not from God but from the creature's origin ex nihilo.
(From l2d44) Obedience to authority is bounded: evil commands must be refused, and tyrants may be resisted collectively but never killed.
